title: The Desolenator: producing clean water

textLines: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 on pages 63 and 64.
Reading Passage 2 has seven sections, A–G.
Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–x, in boxes 14–20 on your answer sheet.
i Getting the finance for production
iii From initial inspiration to new product
iv The range of potential customers for the device
v What makes the device different from alternatives
vi Cleaning water from a range of sources
viii Profit not the primary goal
ix A warm welcome for the device
x The number of people affected by water shortages

Travelling around Thailand in the 1990s, William Janssen was impressed with the basic rooftop solar heating systems that were on many homes, where energy from the sun was absorbed by a plate and then used to heat water for domestic use. Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea he saw in Southeast Asia into a portable device that uses the power from the sun to purify water.

The Desolenator operates as a mobile desalination unit that can take water from different places, such as the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain, and purify it for human consumption. It is particularly valuable in regions where natural groundwater reserves have been polluted, or where seawater is the only water source available. Janssen saw that there was a need for a sustainable way to clean water in both the developing and the developed countries when he moved to the United Arab Emirates and saw large-scale water processing. ‘I was confronted with the enormous carbon footprint that the Gulf nations have because of all of the desalination that they do,’ he says.

The Desolenator can produce 15 litres of drinking water per day, enough to sustain a family for cooking and drinking. Its main selling point is that unlike standard desalination techniques, it doesn’t require a generated power supply: just sunlight. It measures 120 cm by 90 cm, and is easy to transport, thanks to its two wheels. Water enters through a pipe, and flows as a thin film between a sheet of double glazing and the surface of a solar panel, where it is heated by the sun. The warm water flows into a small boiler (heated by a solar-powered battery) where it is converted to steam. When the steam cools, it becomes distilled water. The device has a very simple filter to trap particles, and this can easily be shaken to remove them. There are two tubes for liquid coming out: one for the waste – salt from seawater, fluoride, etc. – and another for the distilled water. The performance of the unit is shown on an LCD screen and transmitted to the company which provides servicing when necessary.

A recent analysis found that at least two-thirds of the world’s population lives with severe water scarcity for at least a month every year. Janssen says that by 2030 half of the world’s population will be living with water stress – where the demand exceeds the supply over a certain period of time. ‘It is really important that a sustainable solution is brought to the market that is able to help these people,’ he says. Many countries ‘don’t have the money for desalination plants, which are very expensive to build. They don’t have the money to operate them, they are very maintenance intensive, and they don’t have the money to buy the diesel to run the desalination plants, so it is a really bad situation.’

The device is aimed at a wide variety of users – from homeowners in the developing world who do not have a constant supply of water to people living off the grid in rural parts of the US. The first commercial versions of the Desolenator are expected to be in operation in India early next year, after field tests are carried out. The market for the self-sufficient devices in developing countries is twofold – those who cannot afford the money for the device outright and pay through microfinance, and middle-income homes that can lease their own equipment. ‘People in India don’t pay for a fridge outright; they pay for it over six months. They would put the Desolenator on their roof and hook it up to their municipal supply and they would get very reliable drinking water on a daily basis,’ Janssen says. In the developed world, it is aimed at niche markets where tap water is unavailable – for camping, on boats, or for the military, for instance.

Prices will vary according to where it is bought. In the developing world, the price will depend on what deal aid organisations can negotiate. In developed countries, it is likely to come in at $1,000 (£685) a unit, said Janssen. ‘We are a venture with a social mission. We are aware that the product we have envisioned is mainly finding application in the developing world and humanitarian sector and that this is the way we will proceed. We do realise, though, that to be a viable company there is a bottom line to keep in mind,’ he says.

The company itself is based at Imperial College London, although Janssen, its chief executive, still lives in the UAE. It has raised £340,000 in funding so far. Within two years, he says, the company aims to be selling 1,000 units a month, mainly in the humanitarian field. They are expected to be sold in areas such as Australia, northern Chile, Peru, Texas and California.
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 21–26 on your answer sheet.

Water is fed into a pipe, and a 22 __________ of water flows over a solar panel. The water then enters a boiler, where it turns into steam. Any particles in the water are caught in a 23 __________. The purified water comes out through one tube, and all types of 24 __________ come out through another. A screen displays the 25 __________ of the device, and transmits the information to the company so that they know when the Desolenator requires 26 __________.

summary: The energy required to operate the Desolenator comes from sunlight. The device can be used in different locations, as it has 21 __________. questions.evidence: Travelling around Thailand in the 1990s ... Two decades later Janssen developed that basic idea ... into a portable device
synonymSubstitutions: initial inspiration ↔ basic idea he saw in Southeast Asia
new product ↔ developed ... into a portable device
distractors: vi is tempting because the final phrase mentions purifying water, but the paragraph’s full progression is from the Thai solar-heating inspiration to Janssen’s later device.
ii, vii and ix describe benefits, production problems or reception that paragraph A never discusses.

questions.evidence: can take water from different places, such as the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain, and purify it for human consumption
synonymSubstitutions: a range of sources ↔ the sea, rivers, boreholes and rain
cleaning water ↔ purify it for human consumption
distractors: x is supported by statistics only in paragraph D, not by this description of water sources.
v focuses on the device’s differentiating selling point, which is paragraph C.

questions.evidence: Its main selling point is that unlike standard desalination techniques, it doesn’t require a generated power supply: just sunlight.
synonymSubstitutions: what makes the device different ↔ main selling point
alternatives ↔ standard desalination techniques
distractors: ii might seem possible because portability is useful, but the paragraph explicitly labels sunlight-only operation as the main selling point.
vii is wrong because the paragraph explains operation, not production difficulties.

questions.evidence: at least two-thirds of the world’s population lives with severe water scarcity ... by 2030 half of the world’s population will be living with water stress
synonymSubstitutions: the number of people ↔ two-thirds ... half of the world’s population
water shortages ↔ severe water scarcity / water stress
distractors: vii is tempting because expensive plants and maintenance are mentioned, but these are access barriers rather than difficulties making the Desolenator.
iv concerns user groups and markets in paragraph E.

questions.evidence: aimed at a wide variety of users – from homeowners in the developing world ... to people living off the grid ... niche markets ... camping, on boats, or for the military
synonymSubstitutions: range of potential customers ↔ wide variety of users
customers ↔ homeowners / people living off the grid / niche markets
distractors: i is about raising production finance, whereas microfinance here is a way for customers to pay.
ix is unsupported: field tests and expected deployment do not describe a warm welcome.

questions.evidence: We are a venture with a social mission ... to be a viable company there is a bottom line to keep in mind
synonymSubstitutions: profit not the primary goal ↔ a venture with a social mission
profit ↔ bottom line
distractors: i is wrong because the paragraph discusses selling prices and mission, not obtaining production funding.
iv belongs to paragraph E’s discussion of user groups.

questions.evidence: It has raised £340,000 in funding so far. Within two years ... the company aims to be selling 1,000 units a month
synonymSubstitutions: getting the finance ↔ raised £340,000 in funding
production ↔ aims to be selling 1,000 units a month
distractors: iv is wrong because named sales regions are not a description of customer types.
ix would require evidence of a positive reception, which paragraph G does not give.

questions.prompt: The device can be used in different locations, as it has 21 __________.
questions.evidence: It measures 120 cm by 90 cm, and is easy to transport, thanks to its two wheels.
synonymSubstitutions: used in different locations ↔ easy to transport
has ↔ thanks to its two
distractors: transport describes the benefit but cannot follow ‘it has’; the required noun copied from the passage is ‘wheels’.
pipe and tubes are components, but they do not explain mobility.

questions.prompt: Water is fed into a pipe, and a 22 __________ of water flows over a solar panel.
questions.evidence: Water enters through a pipe, and flows as a thin film between a sheet of double glazing and the surface of a solar panel
synonymSubstitutions: is fed into ↔ enters through
over a solar panel ↔ between ... and the surface of a solar panel
distractors: thin is only an adjective and cannot fill the noun slot after ‘a’.
sheet refers to double glazing, whereas the flowing layer of water is a film.

questions.prompt: Any particles in the water are caught in a 23 __________.
questions.evidence: The device has a very simple filter to trap particles
synonymSubstitutions: are caught ↔ trap
particles in the water ↔ particles
distractors: boiler converts water to steam but is not stated to trap particles.
pipe carries water into the device; it does not catch particles.

questions.prompt: The purified water comes out through one tube, and all types of 24 __________ come out through another.
questions.evidence: There are two tubes for liquid coming out: one for the waste – salt from seawater, fluoride, etc. – and another for the distilled water.
synonymSubstitutions: purified water ↔ distilled water
all types of ↔ salt from seawater, fluoride, etc.
distractors: salt and fluoride are examples, but neither alone covers ‘all types of’ material from the other tube.
liquid is too general and does not contrast with purified water.

questions.prompt: A screen displays the 25 __________ of the device
questions.evidence: The performance of the unit is shown on an LCD screen
synonymSubstitutions: displays ↔ is shown
device ↔ unit
distractors: information is transmitted by the screen but the specific thing displayed is the device’s performance.
LCD identifies the type of screen and cannot fill the object after ‘displays the’.

questions.prompt: the company so that they know when the Desolenator requires 26 __________.
questions.evidence: transmitted to the company which provides servicing when necessary
synonymSubstitutions: requires ↔ when necessary
they know when ↔ transmitted to the company
distractors: maintenance appears later in paragraph D in a discussion of conventional desalination plants, not what the Desolenator’s company provides.
performance is the preceding blank and is the data transmitted, not the service required.
